Prediction on Test Data for Super Greedy Forests

predict.rfsgt.Rd

Obtain predicted values from a trained super greedy forest. Predictions can be made for new data or, when no new data are given, for the training data, in which case the original forest is restored.

# S3 method for class 'rfsgt'
predict(object, newdata, get.tree = NULL,
        block.size = 10, seed = NULL, do.trace = FALSE,
        node.restrict = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

An object of class (rfsgt, grow) returned by rfsgt.

newdata

Test data. If omitted, the training data are used and the original training forest is restored (see Details).

get.tree

Vector of integers identifying the trees used for the ensemble. By default all trees in the forest are used.

block.size

Controls how the cumulative error rate is computed. The error is recorded after every block.size trees; use an integer between 1 and ntree.

seed

Negative integer specifying the seed for the random number generator.

do.trace

Number of seconds between progress updates on the approximate time to completion.

node.restrict

Logical or NULL, controlling whether lasso terminal nodes use the restricted score (see Details). The default NULL uses the setting saved in the forest. TRUE or FALSE overrides the saved setting for this call only; the forest itself is not changed.

...

Additional options.

Details

To predict an observation, each tree sends the case from the root down to a terminal node. When hcut > 0, the splits and the terminal node predictions are both based on scores. A score is a sparse lasso combination of the dictionary terms, which can include squares, products and higher powers of the variables. With node.center = TRUE, the terms are formed from variables centered at the node. At an internal node, the observation goes to the left daughter if its score is at or below the threshold of the split, and to the right daughter otherwise. Once the observation reaches a terminal node, the node predicts its response using a sparse polynomial estimated by the lasso from the terminal node's inbag cases. When the tree has switched to CART (see rfsgt), the split is a standard CART cut, and the terminal node predicts values using the mean of the inbag responses. With hcut = 0 every node is a CART node, in which case the forest is similar to a random forest.

The function works in two modes. Given newdata, it predicts the new observations. Without newdata, it restores the training forest and reproduces the inbag and out-of-bag predictions of the grow object. Restoring is useful for recomputing the OOB predictions and error rate with a subset of trees (get.tree) or with a different node.restrict setting.

Restricted score

A lasso terminal node score uses a polynomial estimated from its inbag cases. An observation that reaches the node can lie outside the region those cases occupy, and there a square or product can take values that no inbag case produced. The prediction can then fall far outside the range of the response, most often in small trees and at larger hcut.

The restricted score prevents this. With node.restrict = TRUE, each variable is first clamped to its range among the inbag cases of the node, which places the observation at the nearest point of the inbag box. The polynomial is evaluated at that point, and the result is then confined to the range of the inbag responses. The restriction applies to every observation in newdata and, when the training forest is restored, to the out-of-bag observations. Inbag observations are evaluated as usual. The restriction does not change which terminal node an observation reaches, because splits are always evaluated in the ordinary way, and it has no effect on CART terminal nodes. It works the same way with and without node.center.

The default node.restrict = NULL uses the value originally used in the rfsgt training forest call (TRUE by default).

Restoring the training forest

When newdata is omitted, the training data are run down the trees again. For each training observation, predicted averages the trees whose bootstrap sample contains the observation, evaluated exactly as during growth, and predicted.oob averages the remaining trees, using the restricted score when it is on. With the saved node.restrict setting, these reproduce predicted and predicted.oob of the grow object, and err.rate is the OOB error.

Predicting new data

newdata must contain the variables used for training. They are encoded, filtered and expanded into model terms exactly as in training. The response is optional; if present, it is used only to compute err.rate. Every tree in get.tree contributes to the prediction of every observation.

Passing the training data as newdata is not the same as restoring the forest. The observations are then treated as new data. Every tree contributes, including the trees for which an observation was inbag, and the restricted score is applied to every observation. The result therefore matches neither predicted nor predicted.oob of the grow object.

Explaining predictions

get.beta breaks each prediction down into local coefficients and the contributions of the individual terms. For new data, call get.beta(pred, bag = "all", grow = fit), where pred is the prediction object and fit is the grow object.

Value

An object of class c("rfsgt", "predict", family). When newdata is omitted it describes the restored training forest; otherwise it describes the predictions for the new data. The object is a list with the following components.

call

The matched call.

family

Model family of the forest.

n

Number of observations predicted.

samptype

Sampling type used to grow the forest.

sampsize

Bootstrap sample size of each tree.

ntree

Number of trees in the forest.

get.tree

Indices of the trees used for the prediction. get.beta also uses them.

hcut

hcut value of the forest.

node.restrict

Restricted score setting used for this call.

splitrule

Split rule of the forest.

yvar

Response values used to compute the error rate. These are the training responses when the forest is restored, and the response in newdata if it is present; otherwise NULL.

yvar.names

Name of the response.

xvar

Variables of the predicted observations, after the same encoding and filtering as in training.

xvar.augment

Values of the additional model terms (squares, products and higher powers) for the predicted observations, or NULL when the forest uses the variables only.

xvar.names

Names of the retained variables.

xvar.augment.names

Names of the additional model terms, or NULL.

xvar.info

Encoding information used to align new data with the training data.

term.map

Map from each model term to the variables and powers that form it.

leaf.count

Number of terminal nodes in each tree.

forest

The forest used to make the predictions.

membership

Matrix giving the terminal node of each observation in each tree, if membership output was requested; otherwise NULL.

inbag

Matrix of bootstrap counts for each observation and tree, when the forest is restored and membership output was requested; otherwise NULL.

block.size

Block size used for the cumulative error rate.

perf.type

Internal code for the performance measure.

predicted

Predicted values. For new data, the average over the trees in get.tree. For the restored forest, the inbag prediction, which averages the trees whose bootstrap sample contains the observation.

predicted.oob

Out-of-bag predictions when the forest is restored; NULL for new data.

ambrOffset

Internal matrix locating the terminal node of each new observation in each tree, used by get.beta; NULL when the forest is restored.

err.rate

Cumulative mean squared error, recorded after every block.size trees, when response values are available; otherwise NULL.

ctime.internal

Computing time reported by the native code.

ctime.external

Elapsed time measured in R with proc.time().

Author

Hemant Ishwaran and Udaya B. Kogalur

References

Ishwaran H. (2026). Super greedy trees. Artificial Intelligence Review, 59:142. doi:10.1007/s10462-026-11541-6

See also

rfsgt, get.beta, cv.rfsgt

Examples


## ------------------------------------------------------------
##
##  mtcars: for CRAN testing
##
## ------------------------------------------------------------

o <- rfsgt(mpg~., mtcars[1:20,], ntree=3, treesize=1)
p <- predict(o, mtcars[-(1:20),])
print(o)
print(p)

# \donttest{
## ------------------------------------------------------------
##
## train/test using Friedman 3
##
## ------------------------------------------------------------

if (requireNamespace("mlbench", quietly = TRUE)) {

  ## small forest of three trees
  d.trn <- data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(100))
  o <- rfsgt(y ~ ., d.trn, hcut = 1, ntree = 3, treesize = 1)
  print(o)

  ## test set mean squared error
  d.tst <- data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(200))
  y.tst <- d.tst$y
  x.tst <- d.tst[, colnames(d.tst) != "y"]
  yhat <- predict(o, x.tst)$predicted
  mean((yhat - y.tst)^2)

## full forest with hcut = 3
d.trn <- data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(500))
o <- rfsgt(y~.,d.trn, hcut=3)
print(o)

## test set mean squared error on 1000 new observations
d.tst <- data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(1000))
y.tst <- d.tst$y
x.tst <- d.tst[, colnames(d.tst)!= "y"]
yhat <- predict(o, x.tst)$predicted
cat("test set mse:", mean((yhat - y.tst)^2), "\n")

## ------------------------------------------------------------
##
## restore a trained forest using Boston housing
##
## ------------------------------------------------------------

## grow the forest
data(BostonHousing, package = "mlbench")
o <- rfsgt(medv~., BostonHousing)
print(o)

## restore the forest; the OOB error matches the grow object
print(predict(o))

## ------------------------------------------------------------
##
## restored versus test predictions, using Boston housing
## with factors
##
## ------------------------------------------------------------

## turn some of the variables into factors
data(BostonHousing, package = "mlbench")
Boston <- BostonHousing[1:40,]
Boston$zn <- factor(Boston$zn)
Boston$chas <- factor(Boston$chas)
Boston$lstat <- factor(round(0.2 * Boston$lstat))
Boston$nox <- factor(round(20 * Boston$nox))
Boston$rm <- factor(round(Boston$rm))

## grow a single tree and keep the inbag information
o <- rfsgt(medv~., Boston, hcut=2, filter=FALSE, ntree=1, membership=TRUE, nodesize=3)

## predictions from the grow object, from the restored forest, and from
## the training data passed as new data, with and without the
## restricted score
pred <- data.frame(
      inbag=o$inbag,
      pred.inb=o$predicted,
      pred.oob=o$predicted.oob,
      pred.inb.restore=predict(o)$predicted,
      pred.oob.restore=predict(o)$predicted.oob,
      pred.test=predict(o,Boston)$predicted,
      pred.test.unrestricted=predict(o,Boston,node.restrict=FALSE)$predicted)
print(pred)

## Inbag observations are evaluated without the restriction and OOB
## observations with it.  The inbag predictions therefore match the
## unrestricted test predictions, and the OOB predictions match the
## restricted ones.
cat("coherence for inbag data:", sum(pred$pred.inb-pred$pred.test.unrestricted,na.rm=TRUE)==0, "\n")
cat("  coherence for oob data:", sum(pred$pred.oob-pred$pred.test,na.rm=TRUE)==0, "\n")

## train on half of the data and predict the other half
trn <- sample(1:nrow(Boston), nrow(Boston)/2, replace=FALSE)
o.trn <- rfsgt(medv~., Boston[trn,], hcut=2)
print(predict(o.trn,Boston[-trn,]))

## ------------------------------------------------------------
## prediction after tuning hcut and filtering with tune.hcut
## ------------------------------------------------------------

## grow the forest with the tuned hcut and filter
dta <- data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(500))
f <- tune.hcut(y~., dta, hcut=5, verbose=TRUE)
o <- rfsgt(y~., dta, filter=f)
print(o)

## test the tuned forest on new data
print(predict(o, data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(25000))))

## override the tuned hcut
o2 <- rfsgt(y~., dta, filter=use.tune.hcut(f, hcut=2))
print(o2)
print(predict(o2, data.frame(mlbench::mlbench.friedman3(25000))))

}
# }
